variants.title: Read the claim
variants.context: A knowledge graph is claims: an entity is a stable identity (names are attributes, not identifiers); a relationship is a typed, directed claim; a schema says what is allowed; provenance records source, extraction version, confidence, time, and permissions so a claim can be verified or withdrawn.
variants.prompt: Two records both say “J. Smith”. Can the name be the entity identifier?
options: No. Names are attributes; entities need a stable ID such as EMP-104.
Yes, once the two records are matched on their shared employer.
Yes, after normalizing the name to a canonical spelling and case.
optionFeedback: Identity must survive renames and duplicates.
Two colleagues at one employer still collide, and a shared attribute does not create identity.
Normalizing the string makes two different people look identical, and the key still breaks on a rename.
variants.explanation: Names are attributes, not durable identifiers.

variants.title: Read the claim
variants.context: A knowledge graph is claims: an entity is a stable identity (names are attributes, not identifiers); a relationship is a typed, directed claim; a schema says what is allowed; provenance records source, extraction version, confidence, time, and permissions so a claim can be verified or withdrawn.
variants.prompt: An edge WORKS_ON exists but nobody knows whether it means current or past assignment. What is missing?
options: A second WORKS_ON edge pointing in the opposite direction.
Schema semantics: relation meaning, direction, and temporal validity.
Nothing; readers can infer the tense from the source timestamps.
optionFeedback: More edges do not define meaning, and a reversed duplicate makes the direction ambiguous too.
A typed claim needs explicit meaning, direction, and a validity interval.
An ingest timestamp says when the claim was extracted, not what period the assignment covers.
variants.hint: What does the relation type promise?
variants.explanation: Direction and meaning must be explicit.

variants.title: Read the claim
variants.context: A knowledge graph is claims: an entity is a stable identity (names are attributes, not identifiers); a relationship is a typed, directed claim; a schema says what is allowed; provenance records source, extraction version, confidence, time, and permissions so a claim can be verified or withdrawn.
variants.prompt: A claim must be withdrawn after its source turns out to be wrong. What makes that possible?
options: Provenance: source, extraction version, confidence, time, and permissions.
A corroborating edge from a second extractor covering the same fact.
Deleting the entity so every edge touching it disappears with it.
optionFeedback: Provenance lets the system verify or withdraw a claim.
Corroboration raises confidence but does not record which source to invalidate when one is wrong.
The entity may be correct, and deleting it destroys the true claims along with the wrong one.
variants.hint: How do you find every claim from a bad source?
variants.explanation: Every accepted node and edge remains traceable to evidence, policy, and time.

variants.title: Build graph truth
variants.context: Build graph truth in stages: capture source records with text, identity, time, tenant, and access policy; resolve entity identity using stable keys and independent signals; validate relationships for types, direction, corroboration, validity, and conflicts; publish versioned claims with provenance and quarantine weak candidates.
variants.prompt: Extraction proposes new facts from a document. Put the stages in order.

items.text: Validate relationships: endpoint types, direction, confidence, corroboration, temporal validity, conflicts.
Capture the source record: original text, source identity, event time, tenant, access policy.
Publish accepted nodes and edges with provenance; quarantine weak candidates and allow retraction.
Resolve entity identity by matching aliases to canonical IDs with stable keys and independent signals; keep unresolved candidates.

variants.hint: Extraction creates candidates; resolution and validation decide truth.
variants.explanation: The language model may propose facts; it must not silently promote an unsupported claim into graph truth.

variants.title: Build graph truth
variants.context: Build graph truth in stages: capture source records with text, identity, time, tenant, and access policy; resolve entity identity using stable keys and independent signals; validate relationships for types, direction, corroboration, validity, and conflicts; publish versioned claims with provenance and quarantine weak candidates.
variants.prompt: A candidate relation conflicts with an existing fact. Put the stages in order, ending with its fate.

items.text: Its entities resolved to known IDs.
The source record was captured.
Validation detects the conflict with an existing accepted claim.
The candidate is quarantined for review instead of overwriting the graph.

variants.hint: Conflicts go to quarantine, not to production.
variants.explanation: Quarantine weak candidates for review and make retractions possible.

variants.title: Build graph truth
variants.context: Build graph truth in stages: capture source records with text, identity, time, tenant, and access policy; resolve entity identity using stable keys and independent signals; validate relationships for types, direction, corroboration, validity, and conflicts; publish versioned claims with provenance and quarantine weak candidates.
variants.prompt: An alias cannot be matched confidently. Put the stages in order, noting what happens to it.

items.text: Publication excludes the unresolved candidate until it is resolved.
Capture the source record.
Resolution fails to reach the merge threshold; the candidate is preserved unresolved rather than force-merged.
Validation runs for the resolved claims.

variants.hint: Preserve unresolved candidates instead of forcing a merge.
variants.explanation: A forced merge transfers every relationship onto the wrong entity.

variants.title: Resolve identity
variants.context: Entity resolution changes the graph: a false merge transfers every accepted relationship onto the wrong entity; a missed merge creates duplicate islands that hide paths. Thresholds should reflect the cost of a false merge versus the cost of review.
variants.prompt: Two different engineers with the same name are merged. What is the consequence?
options: Traversals get faster because one node replaces two duplicates.
Every relationship of both is transferred onto one wrong entity.
Nothing goes wrong, because the shared name proves they are one person.
optionFeedback: Correctness, not speed, is at stake, and every path through the merged node is now wrong.
A false merge corrupts every path through that node.
Two identical names routinely describe different people, which is exactly the case here.
variants.explanation: A false merge transfers every accepted relationship onto the wrong entity.

variants.title: Resolve identity
variants.context: Entity resolution changes the graph: a false merge transfers every accepted relationship onto the wrong entity; a missed merge creates duplicate islands that hide paths. Thresholds should reflect the cost of a false merge versus the cost of review.
variants.prompt: One employee appears as three unmerged nodes. What is the consequence?
options: Recall improves because three nodes match more queries than one.
Duplicate islands hide paths and split history.
Nothing harmful; the duplicates act as redundant copies of one record.
optionFeedback: Each node matches only its own slice, so every path that crosses the islands is lost.
Missed merges fragment the graph.
The copies are not identical, and connectivity breaks because each island holds different edges.
variants.hint: Can a path cross between the islands?
variants.explanation: A missed merge creates duplicate islands.

variants.title: Resolve identity
variants.context: Entity resolution changes the graph: a false merge transfers every accepted relationship onto the wrong entity; a missed merge creates duplicate islands that hide paths. Thresholds should reflect the cost of a false merge versus the cost of review.
variants.prompt: How should the merge threshold be set?
options: From the cost of a false merge against the cost of manual review.
At a fixed 50 percent name similarity for every entity type.
As high as possible, so no false merge can ever be admitted.
optionFeedback: Thresholds are cost decisions; use stable IDs first, then independent signals.
One fixed similarity ignores cost and treats a rare surname like a common one.
Pushing the threshold up multiplies duplicate islands, and hidden paths cost as much as bad merges.
variants.hint: Which error is more expensive here?
variants.explanation: Combine normalized names with verified attributes and source authority.

variants.title: Shape the query
variants.context: Shape queries around operations: lookup (zero or one hop), neighborhood (bounded expansion), path (a typed route with its chain), aggregate (over a declared subgraph). Bound hop depth and fan-out; filter by tenant, authorization, and validity time during traversal.
options: Path: return the typed route between the service and its owner.
Aggregate: count the owners recorded across the service catalog.
Lookup: a zero or one hop read of the owner property.
optionFeedback: No route needs explaining, because the owner sits on the entity itself.
No population is being counted, and a catalog-wide count does not name this owner.
A direct property read on a single entity.
variants.hint: How many hops does the answer need?
variants.explanation: Increasing depth without a question contract adds noise, latency, and permission risk.

variants.title: Shape the query
variants.context: Shape queries around operations: lookup (zero or one hop), neighborhood (bounded expansion), path (a typed route with its chain), aggregate (over a declared subgraph). Bound hop depth and fan-out; filter by tenant, authorization, and validity time during traversal.
variants.prompt: “Why is Atlas connected to the billing outage?” Which operation, and what must it return?
options: Path: a typed route with the relationship chain behind it.
Lookup: read the direct properties recorded on the Atlas node.
Neighborhood expansion around Atlas with no hop or fan-out limit.
optionFeedback: The chain is the explanation, and it is returned with the answer.
One hop reads attributes and cannot explain a connection several edges away.
Unbounded expansion is not a contract; it returns noise, latency, and paths the asker may not access.
variants.hint: What does the user need to inspect?
variants.explanation: Return path evidence with the answer.

variants.title: Shape the query
variants.context: Shape queries around operations: lookup (zero or one hop), neighborhood (bounded expansion), path (a typed route with its chain), aggregate (over a declared subgraph). Bound hop depth and fan-out; filter by tenant, authorization, and validity time during traversal.
variants.prompt: A traversal filters by tenant only after collecting five hops of neighbors. What is wrong?
options: Nothing; the same rows survive whether the filter runs early or late.
Five hops is too few to reach the tenant boundary reliably.
Filter by tenant, authorization, and validity time during traversal.
optionFeedback: The surviving rows may match, but the traversal already read and expanded through forbidden nodes.
Depth is not the issue; the expansion is crossing into other tenants at every hop.
Post-hoc filtering expands into forbidden territory first.
variants.hint: When does the permission check happen?
variants.explanation: Set maximum hop depth and fan-out for every expansion.

variants.title: Answer with graph evidence
variants.context: Graph RAG: resolve query entities, intent, tenant, allowed relations, hop limit, and freshness; retrieve candidate paths within bounds; attach source passages, timestamps, versions, and permission decisions; reject proposed, stale, contradictory, or inaccessible evidence; generate from the surviving path and cite it, or state the boundary that prevented an answer.
variants.prompt: A question about a service dependency arrives. Put the Graph RAG path in order.

items.text: Reject proposed, stale, contradictory, or inaccessible evidence per the answer policy.
Attach source passages, timestamps, extraction versions, and permission decisions to every candidate claim.
Resolve query entities, intent, tenant, allowed relation types, hop limit, and freshness target.
Generate from the surviving path and cite it, or state which boundary prevented an answer.
Retrieve candidate paths without crossing forbidden edges or expanding an unbounded neighborhood.

variants.hint: The answer is generated only after claims survive policy, freshness, and permission checks.
variants.explanation: The shortest path is not automatically the safest answer.

variants.title: Answer with graph evidence
variants.context: Graph RAG: resolve query entities, intent, tenant, allowed relations, hop limit, and freshness; retrieve candidate paths within bounds; attach source passages, timestamps, versions, and permission decisions; reject proposed, stale, contradictory, or inaccessible evidence; generate from the surviving path and cite it, or state the boundary that prevented an answer.
variants.prompt: The shortest path contains a proposed edge. Put the path in order, ending with the outcome.

items.text: Candidate paths are retrieved, including the short one.
The proposed edge is rejected by policy.
Entities and limits are resolved.
A longer accepted path is used, or the system states the boundary.
Evidence is attached; one edge is marked proposed, not accepted.

variants.explanation: A path can be complete but contain a proposed edge, an expired source, or inaccessible evidence.

variants.title: Answer with graph evidence
variants.context: Graph RAG: resolve query entities, intent, tenant, allowed relations, hop limit, and freshness; retrieve candidate paths within bounds; attach source passages, timestamps, versions, and permission decisions; reject proposed, stale, contradictory, or inaccessible evidence; generate from the surviving path and cite it, or state the boundary that prevented an answer.
variants.prompt: The requester lacks access to a supporting document. Put the path in order, ending with the outcome.

items.text: The inaccessible claim is rejected.
The answer states that an evidence boundary prevented a complete answer.
Attach permission decisions to each claim.
Retrieve candidate paths within bounds.
Resolve entities and the requester’s tenant.

variants.explanation: Enforce tenant and document permissions before a path becomes model context.
